Complex multiplication of elliptic curves

A handful of elliptic curves carry an unreasonably large endomorphism ring — an order in an imaginary quadratic field $K$. These CM curves turn the explicit class field theory of $K$ into geometry: the $j$-invariant generates the Hilbert class field, torsion points generate ray class fields, and Heegner points on $X_0(N)$ encode rational points of analytic rank one on a modular elliptic curve. Heegner numbers, the Gross–Zagier formula, and Stark's conjectures are downstream applications of one quietly remarkable fact.

Reader's note. This page assumes comfort with elliptic curves (Weierstrass form, the chord-tangent law, and the $j$-invariant), with imaginary quadratic fields (orders, ideal class groups), and with class field theory at the level of "Artin reciprocity says the ideal class group governs unramified abelian extensions". The story here is that a single elliptic curve $E/\mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{End}(E)$ bigger than $\mathbb{Z}$ can carry the entire CFT of $K$ on its torsion.

blocks.html:
1. CM elliptic curves over $\mathbb{C}$

Every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{C}$ is uniformized as a complex torus $E = \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ for some lattice $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}\omega_1 + \mathbb{Z}\omega_2$ with $\tau = \omega_2/\omega_1 \in \mathbb{H}$. Its endomorphism ring is

$$\mathrm{End}(E) \;=\; \{\alpha \in \mathbb{C} : \alpha \Lambda \subseteq \Lambda\}.$$

For a generic lattice the only $\alpha$ that scales $\Lambda$ into itself is an integer, so $\mathrm{End}(E) = \mathbb{Z}$. But if $\tau$ satisfies a quadratic relation $a\tau^2 + b\tau + c = 0$ with $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}$ and discriminant $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, then $\tau$ generates an imaginary quadratic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\tau)$, and any $\alpha = u + v\tau \in \mathcal{O}_K$ with $\alpha \Lambda \subseteq \Lambda$ becomes an honest endomorphism. We say $E$ has complex multiplication (CM) by an order $\mathcal{O} \subseteq \mathcal{O}_K$ when

$$\mathrm{End}(E) \;=\; \mathcal{O} \;\supsetneq\; \mathbb{Z}.$$

$j$-invariants of CM points are algebraic integers

The CM locus in $\mathbb{H}$ — the set of $\tau$ generating an imaginary quadratic field — is countable and dense, but not arbitrary. Theorem (Schneider 1937, classical CM theory): if $E/\mathbb{C}$ has CM, then $j(E) \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ is an algebraic integer. The standard examples:

$\tau$order$j(E)$
$i$$\mathbb{Z}[i]$ in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$$1728$
$\rho = e^{2\pi i/3}$$\mathbb{Z}[\rho]$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3})$$0$
$\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-7}}{2}$$\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-7}}{2}]$$-3375$
$\sqrt{-2}$$\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-2}]$$8000$

These integer values are not coincidences. Each corresponds to an imaginary quadratic field of class number $1$, where every fractional ideal is principal — there is essentially only one curve up to isomorphism with that endomorphism ring.

params.bodyScript:
<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.getElementById('cm-tau-svg');
  const out = document.getElementById('cm-tau-out');
  const W = 360, H = 240, X0 = -180;
  // viewBox: x in [-180,180] = Re(tau)*100 ish, y in [0,240] = -Im(tau)*100 (flipped)
  // Map: pixel (px,py) <-> tau = ((px+180)/180 - 1, (240-py)/120)  giving Re in [-1,1], Im in [0,2]
  function pxToTau(px, py){
    const re = (px - 0)/120;
    const im = (H - py)/120;
    return [re, im];
  }
  function tauToPx(re, im){
    return [re*120, H - im*120];
  }
  let tau = [0, 1.0];
  // q-expansion of j(tau): 1/q + 744 + 196884 q + 21493760 q^2 + 864299970 q^3 + ...
  const qCoeffs = [744, 196884, 21493760, 864299970, 20245856256];
  function jApprox(re, im){
    if(im < 0.05) return null;
    // q = exp(2 pi i tau)
    const a = -2*Math.PI*im;       // |q| = exp(-2 pi Im tau), arg q = 2 pi Re tau
    const r = Math.exp(a);
    const ang = 2*Math.PI*re;
    // Sum 1/q + 744 + sum c_n q^n, n>=1
    let re_sum = Math.cos(-ang)/r + 744;
    let im_sum = Math.sin(-ang)/r;
    for(let n=1;n<=qCoeffs.length;n++){
      const cn = qCoeffs[n-1];
      const rn = Math.pow(r, n);
      re_sum += cn * rn * Math.cos(n*ang);
      im_sum += cn * rn * Math.sin(n*ang);
    }
    return [re_sum, im_sum];
  }
  function nearCM(re, im){
    // Detect CM by: does |tau|^2 = m and |2 Re(tau)| = n with m,n small integers?
    const norm = re*re + im*im;
    const trace = 2*re;
    const nN = Math.round(norm);
    const tN = Math.round(trace);
    if(Math.abs(norm - nN) < 0.025 && Math.abs(trace - tN) < 0.025 && nN >= 1){
      // tau is root of x^2 - tN x + nN = 0; disc = tN^2 - 4 nN
      const D = tN*tN - 4*nN;
      if(D < 0) return D;
    }
    return null;
  }
  function draw(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    // axes
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:X0,y1:H,x2:X0+W,y2:H,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.5}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:0,y1:0,x2:0,y2:H,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.5,'stroke-dasharray':'2,3'}));
    // fundamental domain |tau|>=1, |Re tau|<=1/2
    const fd = SVG('path',{
      d:`M ${-60} ${H} L ${-60} ${tauToPx(-0.5, Math.sqrt(3)/2)[1]} A 120 120 0 0 1 ${60} ${tauToPx(0.5, Math.sqrt(3)/2)[1]} L ${60} ${H} Z`,
      fill:'rgba(255,216,102,0.06)', stroke:'var(--yellow)', 'stroke-width':0.6, 'stroke-dasharray':'3,2'
    });
    svg.appendChild(fd);
    // Mark a few CM points
    const cm = [
      {re:0, im:1, lbl:'i'},
      {re:-0.5, im:Math.sqrt(3)/2, lbl:'ρ'},
      {re:0.5, im:Math.sqrt(7)/2, lbl:'(1+√-7)/2'}
    ];
    for(const p of cm){
      const [px,py] = tauToPx(p.re, p.im);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:px,cy:py,r:3.5,fill:'var(--cyan)','fill-opacity':0.6}));
    }
    // Current tau
    const [px,py] = tauToPx(tau[0], tau[1]);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx:px,cy:py,r:6,fill:'var(--yellow)',stroke:'#fff','stroke-width':1.5}));
    const lbl = SVG('text',{x:px+9,y:py-9,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'});
    lbl.textContent = `τ = ${tau[0].toFixed(3)} + ${tau[1].toFixed(3)}i`;
    svg.appendChild(lbl);
    // Readout
    const j = jApprox(tau[0], tau[1]);
    let msg;
    if(!j){
      msg = 'τ too close to real axis; j(τ) diverges as Im(τ) → 0.';
    } else {
      msg = `j(τ) ≈ ${j[0].toFixed(2)} + ${j[1].toFixed(2)}i`;
      const D = nearCM(tau[0], tau[1]);
      if(D !== null){
        msg += `\nCM point detected: τ generates Q(√${D}); End(E) ⊇ Z[τ].`;
        msg += `\nj(τ) is an algebraic integer.`;
      } else {
        msg += `\nGeneric τ: End(E) = Z (no CM).`;
      }
    }
    out.textContent = msg;
  }
  // pointer drag
  let dragging = false;
  svg.addEventListener('pointerdown', e=>{
    dragging = true;
    svg.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
    handleMove(e);
  });
  svg.addEventListener('pointermove', e=>{ if(dragging) handleMove(e); });
  svg.addEventListener('pointerup', e=>{ dragging=false; });
  function handleMove(e){
    const r = svg.getBoundingClientRect();
    const xp = (e.clientX - r.left)/r.width * W + X0;
    const yp = (e.clientY - r.top)/r.height * H;
    const [re, im] = pxToTau(xp, yp);
    if(im > 0.05 && im < 1.95){
      tau = [Math.max(-1.5, Math.min(1.5, re)), im];
      draw();
    }
  }
  document.getElementById('cm-tau-i').addEventListener('click', ()=>{ tau=[0,1]; draw(); });
  document.getElementById('cm-tau-rho').addEventListener('click', ()=>{ tau=[-0.5, Math.sqrt(3)/2]; draw(); });
  document.getElementById('cm-tau-7').addEventListener('click', ()=>{ tau=[0.5, Math.sqrt(7)/2]; draw(); });
  draw();
})();
</script>

Among the $2$-parameter family of lattices, the CM ones form a countable subset, but they are exactly the ones whose $j$-values land in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

2. The Hilbert class polynomial

Fix an imaginary quadratic field $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})$ with discriminant $d_K < 0$ and ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$. There is a bijection

$$\{\text{ideal classes}\,[\mathfrak{a}]\,\text{of}\,\mathcal{O}_K\} \;\longleftrightarrow\; \{\text{isomorphism classes of}\,E/\mathbb{C}\,\text{with}\,\mathrm{End}(E) = \mathcal{O}_K\}, \qquad [\mathfrak{a}] \longmapsto E_\mathfrak{a} = \mathbb{C}/\mathfrak{a}.$$

The set on the right is finite of size $h_K$ (the class number). Their $j$-invariants $j(E_\mathfrak{a})$ are conjugate algebraic integers; the polynomial they all share — the Hilbert class polynomial — is

$$H_K(X) \;=\; \prod_{[\mathfrak{a}]\in\mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_K)} \bigl(X - j(E_\mathfrak{a})\bigr) \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}[X].$$

That the coefficients are rational integers (rather than algebraic integers) is itself a theorem: $H_K$ is the minimal polynomial of $j(E_\mathfrak{a})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, and Galois acts transitively on the set of $j$-values via the class group itself.

The Hilbert class field

Adjoining one root produces the Hilbert class field $H = K(j(E_\mathcal{O_K}))$:

$$H \;=\; K\bigl(j(E_\mathfrak{a})\bigr) \;=\; \text{maximal unramified abelian extension of}\,K.$$

Its Galois group $\Gal(H/K) \cong \mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_K)$ — the class group itself — and the splitting of primes $\mathfrak{p}$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ in $H$ is governed by their image in the class group. This is the explicit class field theory of $K$: the Hilbert class field is generated by a single $j$-value of a CM curve. No abstract Frobenius gymnastics — just compute one transcendental function at one quadratic irrationality.

3. Heegner points on modular curves

The modular curve $X_0(N)$ parametrizes pairs $(E, C)$ where $E$ is an elliptic curve and $C \subset E$ is a cyclic subgroup of order $N$. Its $\mathbb{C}$-points are $\Gamma_0(N) \backslash \mathbb{H}^*$, and its rational points include cusps plus the so-called Heegner points.

A Heegner point on $X_0(N)$ for an imaginary quadratic $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})$ is a pair $(E, C)$ such that both $E$ and $E/C$ have CM by the same order $\mathcal{O}_K$. Equivalently, $\tau \in \mathbb{H}$ satisfies a primitive integer quadratic with $\Gamma_0(N)$-equivalent $\tau$ and $N\tau$ both lying on the CM locus of $K$.

For this to be non-empty, $K$ must satisfy the Heegner hypothesis: every prime $p \mid N$ splits in $K$. Then the Heegner points are exactly

$$\{(\mathbb{C}/\mathfrak{a},\,\mathfrak{a}/\mathfrak{n}) : [\mathfrak{a}] \in \mathrm{Cl}(\mathcal{O}_K),\,\mathfrak{n} \subset \mathcal{O}_K\,\text{with}\,\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{n} \cong \mathbb{Z}/N\}.$$

Why they matter for BSD

Now suppose $E/\mathbb{Q}$ is a modular elliptic curve of conductor $N$ with modular parametrization $\varphi : X_0(N) \to E$. Push a Heegner point $P_K \in X_0(N)(H)$ (where $H$ is the Hilbert class field of $K$) through $\varphi$, and trace down to $E(K)$:

$$y_K \;=\; \mathrm{Tr}_{H/K}\,\varphi(P_K) \;\in\; E(K).$$

The Gross–Zagier formula (1986) asserts that the Néron–Tate height $\hat h(y_K)$ equals an explicit positive multiple of $L'(E/K, 1)$. So:

$$L'(E/K, 1) \ne 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; y_K\,\text{is non-torsion} \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{rank}\,E(K) \ge 1.$$

Combined with Kolyvagin's Euler-system argument, this proves BSD when $\mathrm{ord}_{s=1} L(E/K, s) \le 1$: from a single Heegner point, one constructs the entire rational-points group up to finite index.

<script>
(function(){
  const N = document.getElementById('cm-heeg-N');
  const D = document.getElementById('cm-heeg-D');
  const out = document.getElementById('cm-heeg-out');
  // Class numbers for our test discriminants
  const hData = {'-3':1,'-4':1,'-7':1,'-8':1,'-11':1,'-15':2,'-23':3,'-31':3};
  function legendre(a, p){
    if(p === 2) return null;
    // (a / p) for odd prime p, a integer. Naive Euler criterion.
    if(p === 2) return null; // caller must handle p=2 (Hensel-style D mod 8 test)
    a = ((a % p) + p) % p;
    if(a === 0) return 0;
    const r = modPow(a, (p-1)/2, p);
    return r === 1 ? 1 : -1;
  }
  function modPow(b, e, m){
    let r = 1n;
    b = BigInt(b); e = BigInt(e); m = BigInt(m);
    b %= m;
    while(e > 0n){
      if(e & 1n) r = (r*b) % m;
      e >>= 1n;
      b = (b*b) % m;
    }
    return Number(r);
  }
  function primeFactors(n){
    const out = [];
    for(let p=2; p*p<=n; p++){
      if(n%p===0){ out.push(p); while(n%p===0) n/=p; }
    }
    if(n>1) out.push(n);
    return out;
  }
  function splitsIn(p, d){
    // p splits in Q(√d) iff d is a nonzero QR mod p (for odd p, p∤d)
    if(p === 2){
      // 2 splits in Q(√d) iff d ≡ 1 (mod 8)
      const dmod = ((d % 8) + 8) % 8;
      return dmod === 1;
    }
    if(d % p === 0) return null; // ramifies
    return legendre(d, p) === 1;
  }
  function upd(){
    const Nv = +N.value, Dv = +D.value;
    const ps = primeFactors(Nv);
    let allSplit = true;
    let breakdown = '';
    for(const p of ps){
      const r = splitsIn(p, Dv);
      const tag = r === true ? 'splits' : (r === false ? 'inert' : 'ramifies');
      breakdown += `  p = ${p}: ${tag}\n`;
      if(r !== true) allSplit = false;
    }
    let msg = `K = Q(√${Dv}),  N = ${Nv}\n`;
    msg += `Primes of N: ${ps.join(', ')}\n`;
    msg += breakdown;
    if(allSplit){
      const h = hData[Dv] || '?';
      msg += `\n✓ Heegner hypothesis satisfied. Number of Heegner points (mod Γ_0(N))\n   = h_K · 2^{ω(N)} / |Pic(O_K)/N| ≈ ${h} · 2^${ps.length}.`;
      msg += `\nThe Heegner point P_K ∈ X_0(N)(H) maps to a candidate non-torsion point\nin E(K) for any modular E/Q of conductor N.`;
    } else {
      msg += `\n✗ Heegner hypothesis fails: at least one prime p | N is inert or ramifies in K.\nNo classical Heegner points; need generalized (Shimura curve) construction.`;
    }
    out.textContent = msg;
  }
  N.addEventListener('change', upd);
  D.addEventListener('change', upd);
  upd();
})();
</script>

blocks.html: The widget computes whether the Heegner hypothesis is satisfied and counts the Heegner points modulo $\Gamma_0(N)$. For $N$ prime and split in $K$, the count is exactly $h_K$. The stem of the Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin theorem is that every entry yielding "Heegner hypothesis satisfied" gives a candidate proof of BSD for the corresponding modular elliptic curve, conditional only on $L'(E/K, 1) \ne 0$ — which one can check numerically from the $L$-series.

4. The main theorem of complex multiplication

Class field theory describes abelian extensions of any number field abstractly via the idele class group. For imaginary quadratic $K$ the description becomes explicit — one can write down generators in terms of CM data. This is the content of the main theorem of complex multiplication.

Theorem (Shimura–Taniyama, sharpened from Kronecker, Weber, Hasse). Let $E/\mathbb{C}$ be an elliptic curve with CM by $\mathcal{O}_K$ (so $j(E) \in H$, the Hilbert class field of $K$), and let $\mathfrak{f}$ be an ideal of $\mathcal{O}_K$. Then

$$K(\mathfrak{f}) \;=\; K\bigl(j(E),\, h(E[\mathfrak{f}])\bigr)$$

where $K(\mathfrak{f})$ is the ray class field of conductor $\mathfrak{f}$, and $h$ is the Weber function (essentially the $x$-coordinate, normalized to be Galois-invariant under automorphisms of $E$). The Galois action of $\sigma_\mathfrak{a} = (\mathfrak{a}, K(\mathfrak{f})/K) \in \Gal(K(\mathfrak{f})/K)$ via Artin reciprocity is

$$\sigma_\mathfrak{a} \cdot j(\mathbb{C}/\mathfrak{b}) \;=\; j(\mathbb{C}/\mathfrak{a}^{-1}\mathfrak{b}), \qquad \sigma_\mathfrak{a} \cdot P \;=\; \mathfrak{a}^{-1} \cdot P\,\,(P \in E[\mathfrak{f}]).$$

Reading the formula

Two parallel facts: ideals act on $j$-values by translation in the class group, and on torsion points by ideal multiplication (using the natural $\mathcal{O}_K$-module structure on $E[\mathfrak{f}] \cong \mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{f}$). The first generates $H/K$; the second extends to ray class fields. So:

  • $j$-values give the unramified abelian extension (Hilbert class field).
  • $x$-coordinates of $\mathfrak{f}$-torsion give ramified abelian extensions of conductor $\mathfrak{f}$.
  • Together they exhaust the maximal abelian extension $K^{\mathrm{ab}}/K$.

5. CM abelian varieties (Shimura–Taniyama)

Generalizing from CM elliptic curves to higher dimension: an abelian variety $A$ of dimension $g$ has CM by a number field $L$ of degree $2g$ if $L \hookrightarrow \mathrm{End}^0(A) := \mathrm{End}(A) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$ as a maximal commutative subalgebra. The field $L$ — called a CM field — must be a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field $L_0$ (so $[L:\mathbb{Q}] = 2g$, $[L_0:\mathbb{Q}] = g$).

The CM type is the choice of $g$ embeddings $\Phi = \{\varphi_1, \ldots, \varphi_g\} \subset \mathrm{Hom}(L, \mathbb{C})$ such that $\Phi \sqcup \bar\Phi = \mathrm{Hom}(L, \mathbb{C})$ — a way to pick out which half of the embeddings to use to realise $A$ as $\mathbb{C}^g/\Phi(\mathcal{O}_L)$.

The reflex field and the Shimura–Taniyama formula

Each CM type $(L, \Phi)$ has a reflex field $L^* \subset \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, the field generated by the elementary symmetric functions of $\{\varphi_i(\alpha)\}$ as $\alpha$ ranges over $L$. The reflex defines an "inverse" CM type $(L^*, \Phi^*)$. The main theorem (Shimura–Taniyama 1961) says that if $A$ has CM type $(L,\Phi)$ over $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$, then $A$ is defined over an explicit number field, and Frobenius at a prime $\mathfrak{p}$ of $L^*$ acts on $A$ via

$$\mathrm{Frob}_\mathfrak{p} \;=\; \prod_{\varphi^* \in \Phi^*} \varphi^*(\mathfrak{p})$$

(viewed as an ideal of $L$ via the reflex norm). This recovers all of CM elliptic curve theory when $g = 1, L = K$ imaginary quadratic, $\Phi = \{\mathrm{id}\}$, $L^* = K$. The formula is the bridge from Galois representations of CM abelian varieties to algebraic Hecke characters of the reflex field.

6. Applications: Stark, Heegner numbers, Gross–Zagier

Three landmark consequences of CM theory.

Heegner's class-number-one theorem

Gauss conjectured in 1801 that there are exactly nine imaginary quadratic fields with class number $1$:

$$d \in \{-3,\,-4,\,-7,\,-8,\,-11,\,-19,\,-43,\,-67,\,-163\}.$$

Heegner proved this in 1952 (with a small gap repaired by Birch and Stark in the 1960s) by an ingenious argument using modular equations $\Phi_n(j(\tau), j(n\tau)) = 0$ — direct relations between $j$-values at CM points. The argument runs: if a tenth class-number-1 discriminant existed, $j$-values of CM curves with that discriminant would satisfy modular equations forcing impossible integer factorizations.

The Heegner numbers and $e^{\pi\sqrt{163}}$

For $d \in \{-7, -11, -19, -43, -67, -163\}$ one has $h_K = 1$, so $H_K(X) = X - j(E)$ has a single integer root. Recall $j(\tau) = q^{-1} + 744 + 196884 q + \ldots$ where $q = e^{2\pi i\tau}$. For $\tau = (1+\sqrt{-d})/2$,

$$q = e^{2\pi i \cdot (1+i\sqrt{d})/2} = -e^{-\pi\sqrt{d}}.$$

Substituting into $j$:

$$-e^{\pi\sqrt{d}} + 744 + 196884 \cdot e^{-\pi\sqrt{d}} + \ldots \;=\; j\bigl((1+\sqrt{-d})/2\bigr) \in \mathbb{Z}.$$

For large $d$ the higher-order terms vanish and one gets $e^{\pi\sqrt{d}} \approx 744 - j$, an integer to within $e^{-\pi\sqrt{d}}$. For $d = 163$, $j = -640320^3 = -262537412640768000$, and

$$e^{\pi\sqrt{163}} \;=\; 262{,}537{,}412{,}640{,}768{,}744 - \underbrace{7.5 \times 10^{-13}}_{\text{tiny remainder}}.$$

Gross–Zagier and Stark

The Gross–Zagier formula (1986) computes $L'(E/K, 1)$ for modular elliptic curves twisted by an imaginary quadratic $K$ in terms of the Néron–Tate height of a Heegner point:

$$L'(E/K, 1) \;=\; \frac{8\pi^2 (\varphi, \varphi)}{\sqrt{|d_K|}} \cdot \hat h(y_K).$$

Combined with Kolyvagin's theorem (1989), this proves: for $E/\mathbb{Q}$ modular, if $\mathrm{ord}_{s=1} L(E, s) \le 1$, then BSD's rank conjecture holds. Stark's conjectures pursue the analogous link for $L'(0, \chi)$ and units in abelian extensions; in the imaginary quadratic case (rank-1 abelian Stark) the conjecture is a theorem, and the units are elliptic units built from CM-curve torsion.

Heegner number explorer: $e^{\pi\sqrt{|D|}}$ near-integers
six class-number-one discriminants with $D < -3$

For each discriminant in Gauss's class-number-1 list, $j((1+\sqrt{-|D|})/2)$ is a rational integer (since $h_K=1$). The remainder $e^{\pi\sqrt{|D|}} - (744 - j)$ is bounded by $|196884 \cdot e^{-\pi\sqrt{|D|}}|$ — exponentially small once $|D| \gtrsim 20$.

<script>
(function(){
  const sel = document.getElementById('cm-hn-d');
  const out = document.getElementById('cm-hn-out');
  // j-invariants for class-number-1 discriminants D = -7, -11, -19, -43, -67, -163
  // corresponding to tau = (1+sqrt(-|D|))/2
  const jVals = {
    '-7':   -3375,
    '-11':  -32768,
    '-19':  -884736,
    '-43':  -884736000,
    '-67':  -147197952000,
    '-163': -262537412640768000
  };
  function upd(){
    const D = sel.value;
    const dAbs = -+D;
    const j = jVals[D];
    // e^(pi sqrt(d)) ≈ -q^{-1} where q = -exp(-pi sqrt d)
    // => e^(pi sqrt d) = (744 - j) - 196884 e^{-pi sqrt d} + ...
    const e_pi = Math.exp(Math.PI * Math.sqrt(dAbs));
    const integerEst = 744 - j;
    const remainder = e_pi - integerEst;
    let msg = `|D| = ${dAbs}\n`;
    msg += `j((1+√${D})/2) = ${j}\n`;
    msg += `\n744 − j = ${integerEst}\n`;
    msg += `e^(π√${dAbs})  ≈ ${e_pi.toExponential(15)}\n`;
    msg += `difference   ≈ ${remainder.toExponential(3)}\n`;
    if(Math.abs(remainder) < 1){
      msg += `\nNear-integer to within ${Math.abs(remainder).toExponential(2)}.`;
      msg += `\nHeegner-number phenomenon: q-expansion of j(τ) at\nτ = (1+√${D})/2 forces e^(π√${dAbs}) ≈ 744 − j.`;
    } else {
      msg += `\n(Higher-order q-terms still significant for small |D|.)`;
    }
    out.textContent = msg;
  }
  sel.addEventListener('change', upd);
  upd();
})();
</script>

blocks.html: The "almost-integer" $e^{\pi\sqrt{163}}$ is a popular curiosity, but the underlying mechanism is mathematically deep: the only way $e^{\pi\sqrt{|D|}}$ can land near an integer is if $j((1+\sqrt{-|D|})/2)$ is an integer, which is the case iff $h_K = 1$. Gauss's nine fields make exactly six near-integers (the smaller three are too close to the cusp for the trick to be visible).

Connections

Complex multiplication is the meeting place of three theories that otherwise speak different languages: the explicit class field theory of imaginary quadratic fields (Kronecker's Jugendtraum), the arithmetic of elliptic curves, and the analytic theory of modular forms. The frontier here is Hilbert's 12th problem — generalize the Kronecker–Weber and CM theorems to arbitrary number fields. CM abelian varieties + Shimura varieties give a theory for CM fields; for totally real fields one has Hilbert modular forms and Stark's conjectures, mostly still conjectural.

  • Elliptic curves — Complex uniformization — the $E = \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ description used throughout this page.
  • Class field theory — Hilbert class field — abstract description of the field generated here by $j(E)$.
  • Modular curves — Heegner points — the Gross–Zagier construction's natural home.
  • Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer — Heegner points are the only proven path to BSD for analytic-rank-1 modular curves.
  • Galois representations — CM curves carry abelian Galois representations (algebraic Hecke characters), the "easy case" of Langlands.
  • Iwasawa theory — Coates–Wiles proved the Iwasawa main conjecture in the CM case before the general case was open.
